concept.name: Breakeven inflation
concept.definition: The inflation rate that would make an investor indifferent between holding a nominal Treasury and a same-maturity Treasury Inflation-Protected Security (TIPS), computed as the nominal yield minus the real (TIPS) yield. It is a market-based measure of expected average inflation over the horizon, though it also embeds inflation risk and liquidity premia.
concept.intuition: If nominal bonds pay 4.5% and inflation-protected bonds pay 2.0%, the market is pricing roughly 2.5% average inflation — that gap is the breakeven.
concept.mechanics: Computed from constant-maturity series, e.g. FRED's T10YIE = 10-Year Treasury Constant Maturity (DGS10) minus 10-Year Treasury Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity (DFII10); the latest value implies what market participants expect inflation to average over the next 10 years.
concept.formula: Breakeven inflation ≈ y(nominal, T) − y(real TIPS, T); exactly, (1 + y_nom)/(1 + y_real) − 1 under compounding.
concept.failure_modes: Breakevens mix inflation expectations with inflation risk premia and the liquidity disadvantage of TIPS, so they can diverge from true expectations — e.g. they collapsed in 2008 partly because TIPS became deeply illiquid, not because deflation was genuinely expected.
concept.misconceptions: Breakeven inflation is not a pure forecast of CPI; it is the rate that equates two bond prices, so reading it as the market's literal inflation expectation ignores embedded premia.
concept.example: With the 10-year nominal Treasury at 4.3% and the 10-year TIPS real yield at 2.0%, the 10-year breakeven inflation rate is about 2.3%.

citations.source: FRED, 10-Year Breakeven Inflation Rate [T10YIE] (source: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis)
